components.text: Explain why the contradiction requires rejecting an infinite causal past rather than only the jointly inconsistent arrangement.
Show that independent clock settings make the entire jointly specified configuration possible.
The contradiction identifies an unsatisfiable conjunction, not the impossibility of every infinite causal past.
Independent individual settings do not establish joint satisfiability of the total arrangement.
Justify adopting substantive causal finitism when a logically weaker diagnosis excludes the same contradiction.
Explain why modal independence defeats the logically minimal diagnosis.
The paradox's exclusion does not uniquely warrant the more substantive causal-finitist theory.
Even a modal-independence proposal gains no advantage if both diagnoses exclude the impossible total setup.
Explain why impossibility should be assigned to the infinite-past antecedent rather than only to its conjunction with the setup.
Show why the more substantive causal-finitist diagnosis is warranted despite the proposed minimal alternative.
The disputed issue is whether an infinite past entails the setup's possibility, not merely whether the setup is contradictory.
A valid modal conditional would give causal finitism explanatory work beyond merely excluding the conjunction.
Establish that rearranging or resetting possible components preserves possibility of the resulting total configuration.
Support the first modal premise rather than only its deductive role.
Rearrangement alone does not preserve possibility because possible components can form an impossible configuration.
The conditional needs more than a smooth-rearrangement intuition to license the paradoxical total setup.
Justify transferring individual or independent possibility to the complete infinite joint configuration.
Defend the first conditional premise against a conjunction-only impossibility diagnosis.
Show why the impossible conjunction makes an infinite causal past itself impossible.
Individual possibility and independence cannot transfer possibility to a logically impossible infinite conjunction.
The first conditional premise fails without a justified infinite recombination principle.
Explain why general limits on infinite recombination apply to variation among clocks already coexisting in one possible world.
Answer the claim that component rearrangement or alteration can cross into impossibility.
The relevant demand concerns varying settings of jointly existing clocks, not unrestricted cross-world infinite recombination.
Intrinsic variation of coexisting clocks is claimed to differ from arbitrary structural rearrangement.
Fix comparable background assumptions and account for the prior cost of adding conscious sufferers under bare indifference.
The likelihood comparison must include the auxiliary assumptions needed for conscious sufferers under each hypothesis.
Move beyond abstract probability resources to explain morally permissible divine allowance of severe concrete suffering.
General probability bookkeeping does not supply a morally adequate reason for permitting extreme suffering.
Explain why failure to identify a justifying reason is strong evidence that no divine reason exists.
Show why apparently unnecessary suffering remains substantially less expected under theism.
Finite agents' inability to identify a divine reason does not establish that no morally sufficient reason exists.
Expected ignorance weakens the inference from unexplained suffering to comparative evidence against theism.
Explain why general finite cognitive limits override shared moral knowledge in clear cases of extreme harm.
General expected ignorance does not defeat judgments in clear cases covered by shared moral knowledge.
Determine what positive epistemic standing commonsense intuitions about divine prevention can have without a further philosophical proof.
A commonsense intuition that God would prevent a particular evil can itself justify an evidential judgment.
Provide morally relevant conditions beyond compensation that could distinguish divine permission from direct wrongdoing.
Explain why ordinary judgments against human wrongdoing transfer without qualification to divine creation of a risk-bearing arena.
Creating a voluntary risk-bearing arena may differ morally from personally committing wrongdoing within it.
The argument preserves ordinary prohibitions on wrongdoing while questioning their direct transfer to divine permission.
Specify how worldly observations can confirm or disconfirm theism if unknown divine reasons can accommodate any suffering.
Preserve the evidential role of moral intuitions under the unknown-reasons defense.
Give independently constrained predictions rather than a purpose compatible with any observed harm.
If unknown reasons accommodate every observation, worldly evidence ceases to connect meaningfully with theism.
Preserving some intuitive evidence does not cure a framework that can neutralize every adverse observation.
Purpose-specific possibilities need constraints if they are to preserve confirmation and disconfirmation.
Explain why a valuable risk-bearing arena requires extreme burdens to fall unequally on people who receive few corresponding opportunities.
Show why unknown reasons make this unequal allocation morally expected under perfect theism.
A risk-bearing arena is morally inadequate if severe deprivation is imposed unequally for others' flourishing.
Unknown purposes do not explain why burdens must fall so extremely and unevenly.
Compare suffering under theism and indifference while fixing whether consciousness and relevant background knowledge are already given.
Address whether specific severe and unequal suffering reverses any general likelihood advantage for theism.
State conditions under which suffering can count against rather than always favor theism.
The likelihood comparison changes when consciousness and the resources for adventuresome life are included in the evidence.
Specific forms and distributions of suffering may reverse the broad comparison.
The explicit possibility of reversal preserves evidential sensitivity to richer observations.
Test whether the actual fine-grained form of consciousness fits deliberate divine production better than an accidental natural process.
Explain whether finite embodied agency predicts consciousness's particular fragility and neural dependence.
Fine-grained dependence of consciousness on fragile brain matter may fit accidental production better than divine design.
General goods of finite consciousness do not settle why consciousness has this precarious physical implementation.
